rv.q: Directed by Michael Longhurst with intensity and sensitivity, and performed by a cast that seems to have made a pact to sustain itself at the towering heights achieved early and unfailingly by its mighty star Sharon D Clarke, this Caroline, Or Change is a hurricane wind unleashed on decrepit legacies and newfound cautions.

Caroline's tragedy resonates with a force that takes hold of you by the guts, even more so as Emmie closes the show on a promise of hope, proudly declaring herself the daughter of a maid who repudiates fear.
The chance to believe in change is her hard-won bequest to them — and, in this devastating, uncomfortable, crucial musical, to us.
There is an important musical revival on Broadway that is deeply meaningful, crucial to experience and definitely a necessary change.
The show can’t recover from this intensity; certainly, we cannot.
Should you happen to pass Sharon D Clarke on the street, you might not find her to be a particularly imposing figure.
Caroline, or Change is a masterwork, even in its altered frame.
In the end, the production is clearly saying that Caroline’s existential struggles in this riven, deeply unfair America can be rationalized only as a gift to the next Black generation.
Director Michael Longhurst’s entire lethargic production, brought here from Britain, denies her the snowballing buildup that would ensure a big payoff in the end.
There's so much to cherish in this miracle of a musical, its puzzle-box structure, thematic patterning, and — you're not ready —its shocking release with the eleventh-hour number, 'Lot's Wife.'
“Caroline, or Change” ought to be better appreciated today.

Co-directors James Robinson and Camille A. Brown create a sweeping epic production, highlighted by an explosive step-dancing routine, which would stop any Broadway show, choreographed with dazzle by Brown.
This production stakes a claim for the musical as an essential classic, iconic in both its scope and execution.
The collision of musical styles and Kushner’s clever, witty lyricism makes Caroline, Or Change a haunting, unforgettable musical.

What makes this work so powerful, and especially timely, is how this splendid cast tells a small story about change – literal pocket change – while offering a larger glimpse into the complex undercurrents in a tense moment of change in American history.
It’s not easy to juggle despair and exuberance without resorting to sentimentality, and Caroline still manages the task handily.
Michael Longhurst’s gorgeous revival of Caroline, or Change, now running at Studio 54, proves that it was well worth the wait.
Longhurst’s production, along with the choreography by Ann Yee, is somewhat more earthy and musical-comedy-flashy than George C. Wolfe’s delicately ethereal original.
That song and its show-stopping performance is a few minutes that, pardon the pun, will be life-changing for many of the people lucky enough to experience it.
Longhurst’s staging, supplemented by Ann Yee’s minimal choreography, is exceptional.
This incredible musical has finally come into its own.
Longhurst's revival is strongly sung, led by the astounding vocals of Sharon D. Clarke in the title role.
It is an excellently constructed show, its message surviving mostly intact.
Clarke animates a curious — and at times troubling — musical with undeniable life.
It all makes for one massive scrambled egg of a narrative.
This journey is one everyone must take sooner than later.
The first Broadway revival of this challenging 2004 musical makes a sincere but ultimately unpersuasive case.
All the performers are better than the script.
I believed in next to nothing of what I saw in this revival.

tn.cat: Best Costume Design of a Musical

cn.t: Critics hail this revival of Kushner and Tesori's 2003 musical as overdue recognition for an underappreciated masterwork, with near-universal praise for Sharon D Clarke's towering, transcendent performance as Caroline.

vs.sum: The legendary former nightclub retains a distinctive atmosphere even in its theatrical configuration. However, comfort is among the worst on Broadway — the rear mezzanine is extremely steep with limited guardrails and tight legroom throughout both levels.

acc.note: No elevator to Mezzanine. 10 induction loops. 81 assistive listening devices. Orchestra wheelchair seating.
